title: OOP, SOLID & Patterns You Actually Use

scenes.say: Your checkout is a forty line if chain, and a new payment method is due Monday. How do you add it without breaking the others? By the end you'll know, and name the pattern.
Today you'll do three things. Replace an if chain with classes. Name strategy, factory, observer and injection. And explain SOLID with an example.
lines: Replace an if chain with classes.

scenes.title: Add a payment method safely
scenes.statement: Checkout is one if/elif chain. Add crypto without editing the old branches.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. Checkout is one long if chain. For example, card, paypal, and now crypto is due. The answer: a new class, and zero edits to the old branches.

scenes.head: The wall socket
scenes.say: Think of a wall socket. A lamp plugs in. A laptop plugs in. Tomorrow you buy a kettle, and it plugs in too. Nobody rewires the wall. The socket is an interface, and good object oriented design gives your code sockets like that.

scenes.head: The smell
scenes.say: Here's our checkout. It works, and prints paypal fifty. But every new method means editing this function again, and risking the old branches. Most candidates stop here and call it done. That is the smell: one function that must change for every new rule.

scenes.head: One class per rule
scenes.say: That's our answer to the problem. Each rule is its own class. The base class is the socket: it promises a pay method. Card keeps its rule. PayPal keeps its own. That's the strategy pattern.

scenes.head: Checkout stays the same
scenes.say: Checkout takes any strategy and calls pay. It never asks which one. Hand it a card: card fifty. Hand it PayPal: paypal fifty. Same checkout, different behavior, and no if chain.
Your turn. Product asks for a third method, crypto. You write a Crypto class with a pay method. Which existing code has to change?
scenes.q: You add `class Crypto(PaymentStrategy)`. What existing code changes?

scenes.head: Open to extension
scenes.say: Nothing. Crypto just plugs into the same socket, and checkout runs it unchanged. That is open closed: open to extension, closed to modification. You add code instead of editing code that already works.

chapters.title: SOLID, one habit at a time

scenes.title: Explain SOLID with an example
scenes.statement: Five principles, one line each, shown on our checkout. Then the follow-ups.
scenes.say: Here's the problem. The interviewer says: explain SOLID, with an example. For example, we use our checkout. The answer: five one-liners, each tied to code. Never recite without an example.

scenes.head: SOLID on our checkout
scenes.say: Five letters, each one line. Single responsibility: the checkout charges, a mailer emails. Open closed: add a class, don't edit. Liskov: a subclass works anywhere its parent does. Interface segregation: small interfaces, not one giant one. Dependency inversion: depend on the socket, not the details.
rows: small interfaces, not one giant one
depend on the socket, not details

scenes.head: Breaking Liskov
scenes.say: Here's the habit candidates break. A Penguin is a Bird, so we subclass. But Penguin's fly raises an error. Migrate takes birds and calls fly on each. Pass it a penguin, and the parent's promise breaks.
Which principle did that Penguin break? Pause and pick.
scenes.q: Penguin.fly() raises. Which principle is broken?

scenes.head: The fix: split the family
scenes.say: Liskov. A penguin can't stand in for a flying bird. The fix: Bird no longer promises to fly. Only FlyingBird does. Sparrow inherits from it. Penguin doesn't, so migrate never receives one.

scenes.head: The four pillars
scenes.say: Interviewers also ask for the four pillars. Encapsulation: hide the data behind methods. Abstraction: expose only what callers need. Inheritance: reuse a parent. Polymorphism: one call, many behaviors, like pay.

scenes.head: Judgment calls
scenes.say: Inheritance or composition? Prefer composition: hold a part instead of being one. When to inherit? Only for a true is a relationship. Is SOLID always right? No. Wait for the second case before abstracting.
rows: no: wait for the 2nd case first

scenes.title: Who picks the strategy?
scenes.statement: A config string says "paypal". Turn it into the right object, in one place.
scenes.note: Callers must not know the classes
scenes.say: Here's the problem. Config gives us a string. For example, paypal. We need the matching object. And callers shouldn't know which class it is.

scenes.head: Who builds the strategy?
scenes.say: A config file says paypal. It's a string. A factory turns it into a PayPal object. Skip it, and the if chain returns.

scenes.head: Factory: one place that picks
scenes.say: A factory is a function that decides which object to build. Give it a name like paypal and it looks it up in a dict, then builds the strategy. Callers never know which concrete class they got. All the choosing lives in one place.
Predict. A customer picks bitcoin, which isn't in the dict. We call make payment with bitcoin. What happens?

scenes.head: Fail loudly
scenes.say: A KeyError, and it names the missing key. Good: a typo in config stops the program, instead of charging the wrong method. In real code, catch it and raise a ValueError with a friendlier message.

scenes.title: React and test without coupling
scenes.statement: A paid order must trigger email and stock, and tests must not charge real cards.

example.output: no edits to Order; test in ms

scenes.say: Here's the problem. When an order is paid, email and stock must react. For example, add analytics later. We want zero edits to Order, and tests in milliseconds.

scenes.head: Observer: publish, react
scenes.say: Now a payment succeeds. Email, stock and analytics all care. The order shouldn't know them. Observer: the order keeps a list of subscribers, and when it's paid, it calls each one. It never knows who's listening.

scenes.head: Observer in nine lines
scenes.say: The order keeps a list. Subscribe adds a function to it. When the order is paid, it loops over the list and calls each one. Subscribe an email function, pay, and the email goes out.
Predict. Email and stock already subscribe. Marketing wants analytics too. Which existing code in Order changes?
scenes.q: Add an analytics subscriber. What changes inside `Order`?

scenes.head: Add a listener, edit nothing
scenes.say: Nothing. Analytics just subscribes, and the next paid call reaches it. The cost is hidden coupling: you can't see who reacts by reading Order. Forget to unsubscribe, and dead listeners keep getting calls.

scenes.head: Dependency injection
scenes.say: Last pattern. Dependency injection: a class receives what it needs instead of building it. Checkout takes its gateway in the constructor. In production, pass the real one. In a test, pass a fake that answers at once.

scenes.head: Why inject? Speed and safety
scenes.say: Run the same checkout twice. The real gateway sleeps half a second, standing in for a network call, and it would charge a real card. The fake answers in no time. Same code, fast and safe.

panels.code:
for g in (RealGateway(), FakeGateway()):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    assert Checkout(g).run(50) == "ok"
    print(type(g).__name__, round(
        time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")

scenes.head: Say it in 25 seconds
scenes.say: SOLID, with an example? An if chain becomes one class per rule. Liskov? A subclass works wherever its parent does. Inherit or compose? Compose unless truly is a. Four pillars? Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism. Always right? No. Wait for a second case.

scenes.head: Say it in 25 seconds
scenes.say: Strategy versus an if chain? Swap behavior without editing old code. Why a factory? Creation logic lives in one place. Observer risk? Hidden coupling, forgotten unsubscribes. Why inject? A fake makes tests fast and safe. And say where you used one.

scenes.head: Try these this week
scenes.say: Three exercises. Find an if chain in your own code and turn it into strategies. Add an observer so one event triggers two reactions. Write a test with a fake gateway and time it.
rows: Make one event notify two listeners
Test checkout with a fake gateway, time it

scenes.say: So say this. Depend on small interfaces, not details. Strategy swaps behavior, a factory picks it, injection hands it in. Observer lets many react to one event. Always name where you used it.
lines: Small interfaces, not details; extend, don't edit.
Strategy swaps, factory picks, injection hands in.
Observer: many react to one event.
